title: Pest evidence, waste and by-product management
audience: Cleaners on food-processing sites who handle waste and may see pest evidence.
learningOutcomes: Recognise signs of pest activity and improperly contained waste.
Segregate food by-product streams so that waste does not contaminate ingredients or packaging.
Preserve evidence and refer unidentified pest contamination or regulated waste, without disturbing it.

instruction.heading: Why pests and waste belong in the same lesson
instruction.body: Pests and waste are linked. Rodents, insects and birds are drawn to food residue and to waste that is not sealed, and they can carry harmful micro-organisms into the areas where food is handled. The FSANZ pest guidance places the obligation with the operator. Under Standard 3.2.2, the operator is expected to take every reasonable step that keeps pests out of the premises and clears out any that get in, including from vehicles that carry food. It is not a duty that a cleaner can discharge by acting alone. Your job on a food site is to notice, protect and refer. You are not the pest-control provider, and you are not the person who decides how waste is classified or moved. Keep that boundary clear from the first shift.

instruction.heading: Recognising pest signs and loose waste
instruction.body: Pest evidence takes several forms. Look for droppings, gnawing on packaging, timber or cable sheathing, nesting material, shed skins, live or dead insects, trails in dust or grease, and an unusual smell that does not match the product. Insects may appear as small clusters near drains, under bins or in the seams of stored packaging. Waste that is not contained is also a warning sign. Watch for lids left open, bags that are split or torn, bins that are overfull, residue on the floor beneath a bin, and waste stored close to ingredients, packaging or a wash-down point. The FSANZ guidance recommends that a pest management plan names the areas to inspect, such as behind equipment and inside cupboards, and that traps and bait stations are placed away from food and food-contact surfaces, with a site map. Check these areas as part of your normal walk, but do not disturb a station or trap that is not yours to service. Report it instead.

instruction.heading: Segregating by-product streams
instruction.body: Food processing produces several streams of material: edible by-product that the site has approved for a defined use, inedible food waste, general waste, packaging, recyclables, and regulated or chemical waste. Each stream needs its own labelled container, its own route and its own holding point. The reason is simple. When streams are mixed, a single contaminated item can carry risk into ingredients, packaging or a clean zone. The contamination controls in the Safe Food Australia guide (p. 35) also keep chemicals for cleaning and pest control away from food processing areas, which means a waste route should not pass a chemical store or a pest-control station. Plan your route before you start. Use the approved path that keeps waste away from exposed product and wrapped packaging, and avoid carrying a full bin across a clean line. Storage of garbage is covered in Standard 3.2.3, which the guide locates under the garbage storage clause; the wording of that clause was not read for this draft, and it should be checked against the current standard.

instruction.heading: Preserving evidence and referring
instruction.body: Pest evidence is information for the people who investigate and control pests. If you sweep up droppings, empty an unidentified container or move a nest, you destroy the record of where the activity was and you may spread material. Preserve the scene where it is safe to do so. Close off the immediate area so that work and foot traffic do not move the evidence, and keep people from entering the zone without the responsible person's approval. Do not apply a pest-control product yourself. Record the location, the time, what you saw, how you know, who you told and what action you withheld. If the site's procedure allows photographs, take them without moving items. Then refer the matter to the authorised person and record the hold, the pending decision and the name of the person who will decide next. A hold is not a finding that the area is contaminated, and it is not a clearance. It means the question is open and the responsible person must answer it.

instruction.heading: Regulated waste and unknown containers
instruction.body: Some waste is regulated because of what it contains, how it reacts or how it can harm people or the environment. A cleaner does not classify waste, decide its route or choose a waste contractor. Those decisions sit with the site's waste procedure and the lawful waste contractor. Victoria's current EPA page on transporting hazardous waste places a general environmental duty on those who carry waste, asks that drivers be trained, and requires that some priority waste be logged in an online tracker and covered by a permission. That guidance is Victorian and is included here only as an example of the kind of control that applies. If a container is unlabelled or its contents are unknown, do not open it, add to it or move it. Stop, record and refer.

instruction.heading: Pest-control products and who may use them
instruction.body: Pest-control products are regulated. The FSANZ guidance expects a food business to pick products that suit food premises and to keep their labels in view, and it treats pest control as a managed program in which inspections and treatments are logged and any recommended fix is acted on without delay. Only the people authorised by the business and, where required, licensed under state or territory rules may apply a pesticide. A cleaner who finds evidence reports it. A cleaner does not treat it. Where the pests cannot be managed through the site's own program, the business is expected to call in professional help, and that call is made by the authorised person, not by the cleaner.

procedure: Before starting, confirm the zone, the waste streams in use and the authorised person for pest and waste matters.
Look for pest signs and loose waste as you work, using the site map and the inspection areas named in the pest management plan.
Keep each waste stream in its own labelled container, and use only the approved route and holding point.
Keep waste sealed, and do not overfill a container or leave a lid open.
If you find pest evidence or an unknown container, stop work in that zone, keep people out where it is safe, and do not sweep, empty, open or treat the material.
Record the location, time, observed condition, how you know, who you told and the action withheld.
Refer the matter to the authorised person, and record the hold and the pending decision.
Do not resume work in the zone until the authorised person has confirmed in writing how the matter will be handled.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner finds droppings beside a bin of food by-products, close to a stack of wrapped packaging. The bin lid is open. (Example scenario; the site, bin and quantities are fictional.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do first, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not sweep the droppings, move the packaging or close the lid as a tidy-up. Keep people away from the stacked packaging where it is safe, and do not use the bin until the authorised person has seen the scene. Record the zone, the time, the signs seen, the open lid and the packaging position. Refer to the authorised person, and record the hold and who will decide the next step. The record does not say the area is contaminated or clear.

workedExamples.situation: A split bag of by-product sits on a pallet beside the wrapping line. A colleague asks you to carry it to the dock quickly, through the wrapping area, so that the line can keep running. (Example scenario.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which route do you use, and who do you involve?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not carry the split bag through the wrapping area. The approved route is the one that keeps waste away from exposed packaging, and the site decides it. Contain the spill with the approved material if you are trained to do so, keep the bag closed, and ask the supervisor to confirm the route. Record the split bag, the pallet location, the decision and the person who confirmed the route. Speed on the line is not a reason to change the route.

workedExamples.situation: An unlabelled drum with a loose lid sits near the store of by-product bins. Its contents are unknown. The supervisor says it is probably the same as the other drums. (Example scenario.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can you accept the supervisor's assumption?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. An unknown container is a stop condition. Do not open the drum, move it or add to it, and do not accept a guess about its contents as a basis for handling. Keep people clear of the drum where it is safe, record its location, the label status, the lid condition and the supervisor's statement as an unverified assumption. Refer the drum to the competent person and the authorised waste route, and hold the zone until they decide.

equipmentAndPpe: Labelled containers for each waste stream, with lids that close.
Site map showing inspection areas, trap and bait positions, and the approved waste routes.
Gloves and eye protection as set by the site procedure and the SDS for any cleaning product used.
Closed footwear and clean outer clothing, changed if contaminated.
Evidence and referral record form, with space for time, location and the hold.
Camera, only where the site procedure allows and only without moving the evidence.
Spill kit with the approved absorbent, held by the site and used only if trained.

commonErrors.error: Sweeping droppings into a bin, or tidying the area before anyone sees it.
commonErrors.prevention: Preserve the evidence where it is safe, record it, and refer it to the authorised person.

commonErrors.error: Carrying waste past packaging or ingredients to save time.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only the approved route, and ask the supervisor to confirm it before moving anything.

commonErrors.error: Mixing streams because one container is nearly full.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the container for its own stream, or stop and ask for another container.

commonErrors.error: Applying a pest-control product, or moving a trap, without authority.
commonErrors.prevention: Pest control is carried out only by the people authorised by the site. Report and refer.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a sighting is old and does not need recording.
commonErrors.prevention: Record every sighting with its time and location, and let the authorised person decide its age and significance.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The FSANZ Pests page (updated 30 September 2025) describes the Standard 3.2.2 pest obligation as resting with the operator, who must take reasonable action against pests in the premises and in vehicles that carry food. An individual cleaner does not carry that obligation.

Pest-control products used on food premises should be approved for that use and should carry safety and expiry information. A cleaner must not apply, mix or move these products. This lesson does not authorise any pesticide use or pest-control work.
Licensing, training and record rules for people who apply pesticides differ between states and territories.

The contamination controls on p. 35 of the Safe Food Australia guide (Nov 2024 revision) keep chemicals for cleaning and pest control out of food processing areas. A waste route should not pass through them.

Transporting regulated or hazardous waste can require permits, training and tracking. In Victoria, the EPA page on transporting hazardous waste (updated 14 May 2025) places the general environmental duty on carriers, asks for driver training, and requires logging and permissions for some priority waste. This lesson does not grant any transport permit or waste authority.

qualityStandard: Pest signs and loose waste identified on the simulated site drawing, with each sign linked to its zone.
Waste streams kept in separate labelled containers, with the approved route named in the practical.
Evidence preserved and referred in the case study without disturbance, and the hold recorded with a pending decision.
No pest-control product applied, and no unknown container opened, in any part of the exercise.
documentationEvidence: Pest evidence and location record, with date, time, zone, signs observed and how they were identified.
Waste stream and route record for the shift, showing the approved route used.
Referral and hold record, naming the authorised person and the pending decision.
summary: The business must prevent and eradicate pests; the cleaner recognises, protects and refers.
Keep waste streams apart and use only the approved route, away from ingredients and packaging.
Preserve evidence without disturbing it, record the hold, and let the authorised person decide.

knowledgeChecks.question: You find droppings near food by-products. What is the correct first action?
options: Sweep them into the bin, since the droppings are small and easy to remove quickly from the floor
Preserve the evidence where safe, record the location and time, and refer it to the authorised person
Apply a pest product from the store, since it is the quickest way to deal with the droppings found

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must waste streams be kept apart on a food site?
options: For tidiness only, so the bins look neat on the production floor
Because the containers look the same and the labels can be ignored
So that waste cannot carry contamination to ingredients or packaging

knowledgeChecks.question: A drum with no label is beside the by-product bins. What is correct?
options: Open it to check the contents, so the team knows what is inside it before moving it
Accept a colleague's guess about the contents and move it to the dock for collection
Stop, keep people clear where safe, record it, and refer it to the competent person
